q: Which organelle is the site of photosynthesis in a plant cell?
why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs the light energy used in photosynthesis.

q: Which enzyme breaks down starch into maltose?
why: Amylase digests starch. Protease acts on protein and lipase acts on fats.

q: Which substance in red blood cells carries oxygen around the body?
why: Haemoglobin binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the tissues.

q: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine?
why: A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

q: Water moves across a partially permeable membrane from a region of high water concentration to a region of low water concentration. What is this called?
why: That is the definition of osmosis. Diffusion covers the movement of other particles.

q: How many daughter cells does one cell produce by meiosis?
why: Meiosis makes four genetically different cells, each with half the chromosome number.

q: What is the name of the process by which plants lose water vapour through their leaves?
why: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the plant, mainly through the stomata.

q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure. Veins carry it back.

q: Which part of the cell controls its activities and contains the DNA?
why: The nucleus holds the chromosomes and controls the activities of the cell.

q: Which gas is released as a by-product of photosynthesis?
why: Plants take in carbon dioxide and water and release oxygen.

q: What is an organism that makes its own food from simple inorganic substances called?
why: Producers, such as green plants, make their own food. Consumers feed on other organisms.

q: Two heterozygous parents (Tt × Tt) have offspring. What fraction are expected to show the recessive trait?
why: Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt, so one in four offspring show the recessive trait.

q: What is the function of ribosomes?
why: Ribosomes read mRNA and join amino acids together to make proteins.

q: Which cell structure controls what enters and leaves the cell?
why: The cell membrane is partially permeable and regulates the movement of substances in and out.

q: Which molecule is the main energy currency of the cell?
why: ATP releases energy when its terminal phosphate is removed and is used for most cell activities.

q: Which organelle releases most of a cell's energy in aerobic respiration?
why: Most ATP is produced in the mitochondria during the later stages of aerobic respiration.

q: What is the name for an enzyme's special region where the substrate binds?
why: The shape of the active site fits one substrate, which makes enzymes specific.

q: What happens to most enzymes if the temperature gets too high?
why: High temperature changes the shape of the active site, so the enzyme stops working.

q: Which sugar is the main product of photosynthesis?
why: Photosynthesis makes glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy.

q: Where in a chloroplast does the light-dependent stage take place?
why: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes of the grana.

q: Which gas is taken in by plants for photosynthesis?
why: Carbon dioxide enters leaves through stomata and is used to make glucose.

q: What is the correct word equation for aerobic respiration?
correct: Glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water + energy
why: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to release energy from glucose, producing carbon dioxide and water.

q: What is produced when yeast respires anaerobically?
why: Yeast ferments glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide when there is no oxygen.

q: Which organ produces bile?
why: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

q: What does bile do in digestion?
why: Bile breaks large fat droplets into smaller ones, giving lipase a larger surface area to work on.

q: Where does most absorption of digested food take place?
why: The small intestine has villi that give a very large surface area for absorption.

q: Which part of the blood fights infection by engulfing pathogens?
why: Phagocytes are white blood cells that engulf and digest pathogens.

q: Which blood component is mainly involved in clotting?
why: Platelets help form a clot at a wound by triggering the production of fibrin.

q: Which chamber of the heart pumps blood to the whole body?
why: The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood around the body.

q: Which vessels carry blood from the heart to the lungs?
why: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.

q: What is the job of the valves in the heart and veins?
why: Valves keep blood moving in one direction.

q: Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
why: Alveoli have thin walls and a large surface area for oxygen and carbon dioxide to diffuse across.

q: Which muscle contracts and flattens when we breathe in?
why: The diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out, so air is drawn into the lungs.

q: Which organ filters the blood and produces urine?
why: The kidneys remove urea and excess water and salts from the blood to form urine.

q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose levels?
why: Insulin, made in the pancreas, causes cells and the liver to take up glucose.

q: Which gland is known as the master gland of the body?
why: The pituitary gland releases hormones that control many other glands.

q: What is the name of the gap between two neurons?
why: Chemicals called neurotransmitters cross the synapse to pass the signal on.

q: Which part of the brain controls balance and coordination?
why: The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.

q: A reflex action is best described as:
why: A reflex does not need to be thought about, which makes it quick and protective.

q: Which type of cell division produces gametes?
why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make sex cells.

q: What is the role of mitosis?
why: Mitosis makes genetically identical daughter cells for growth and repair.

q: What is the shape of a DNA molecule?
why: DNA is two strands of nucleotides twisted into a double helix.

q: What name is given to a section of DNA that codes for a protein?
why: A gene is a length of DNA with the code for a particular protein.

q: What are different forms of the same gene called?
why: Alleles occupy the same position on homologous chromosomes.

q: Which term describes an organism with two identical alleles for a gene?
why: A homozygous organism has two copies of the same allele.

q: Where is DNA found in a human cell?
why: In eukaryotic cells most DNA is in the chromosomes in the nucleus.

q: What does mRNA do?
correct: Carries the code from DNA to the ribosome
why: mRNA is copied from DNA in transcription and carries the code to a ribosome.

q: Which scientist is known for using pea plants to study inheritance?
why: Mendel's pea plant experiments led to the basic laws of inheritance.

q: What word describes the process of natural selection leading to change over generations?
why: Organisms best suited to their environment survive and pass on their genes, so a population changes over time.

q: What is a population?
correct: All the members of one species living in an area
wrong: All the species in an area
All the organisms and their habitat
All the plants in a forest
why: A population is a group of the same species living in the same place.

q: What is an ecosystem?
correct: A community and its non-living environment
wrong: A group of the same species
A place with no living things
why: An ecosystem is the community of living things together with their abiotic environment.

q: Which of these is a decomposer?
why: Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

q: In a food chain, which organisms are always the first link?
why: Producers make their own food, usually by photosynthesis, and start the food chain.

q: What does a pyramid of numbers show?
correct: The number of organisms at each trophic level
why: Each bar represents how many individuals are at that feeding level.

q: Which is an abiotic factor?
why: Abiotic factors are non-living, such as light, temperature and pH.

q: What is the name for plant water loss through the leaves?
why: Water evaporates from the leaves through the stomata, pulling more water up the xylem.

q: Which tissue carries water up a plant?
why: Xylem vessels carry water and minerals from roots to leaves.

q: Which structures control the opening and closing of stomata?
why: Guard cells change shape to open or close the stomata.

q: What is the function of root hairs?
why: Root hairs increase the surface area for absorption.

q: What is the correct order of the stages in the life of a flowering plant seed?
why: A seed germinates, the plant grows and flowers, and fertilisation then forms new seeds.

q: What is pollination?
correct: Transfer of pollen from anther to stigma
wrong: Growth of a pollen tube only
why: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to a stigma, which comes before fertilisation.

q: Which microbe is used to make bread rise?
why: Yeast produces carbon dioxide in fermentation, which makes the dough rise.

q: Which organism produces the antibiotic penicillin?
why: Alexander Fleming found that Penicillium mould killed bacteria.

q: What is the purpose of a restriction enzyme in genetic engineering?
correct: To cut DNA at specific sequences
why: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific base sequences, leaving ends that can be joined to other fragments.
